extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style and usage guide offering terminology, reporting guidance, and sensitivity notes for covering diverse communities and sensitive topics in news reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: suicide
rubrics_metrics.description: Suicides usually result from a confluence of events and circumstances; mental health disorders and/or substance abuse are associated with 90 percent of suicides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid citing a single cause (e.g., 'recent money woes' or 'a fight with a spouse'). Even family and friends may not recognize warning signs. For more information, consult resources such as Reporting on Suicide, CDC Suicide Facts at a Glance, and Dart Center resources (In Depth: Covering Suicide, Tip Sheets including military/veteran, college campuses, suicide and the media).

rubrics_metrics.name: suicide bombing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of explosives carried to a target on the body of the attacker or in a vehicle operated by him or her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially fearsome because the attacker cannot be bargained with; compared to WWII kamikaze attacks. Thought to have been invented in the early 1980s by the Tamil Tigers in Sri Lanka.

rubrics_metrics.name: suicide contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of news coverage can increase the likelihood of suicide in vulnerable individuals; magnitude relates to amount, duration and prominence of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk increases when stories explicitly describe the suicide method, use dramatic/graphic headlines or images, or sensationalize/glamorize the death. Suicide contagion (copycat suicide) occurs when reporting contributes to another suicide. See suicide entry for responsible coverage guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunni
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'SOO-nee.' The largest denomination in Islam, followed by about 85 percent of Muslims. The plural form is Sunnis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Shiism, Shiite for related entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: swastika
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most popular symbols for Hindus, Jains and Buddhists; word derived from Sanskrit meaning 'auspicious' and 'well-being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in many religious/civil ceremonies in India; the Nazi swastika was a perverted version of the ancient Hindu swastika. Context matters when reporting on the symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: systemic racism
rubrics_metrics.description: Social values that support personal and institutional discrimination; explains how people of color must adapt to a society not built for them while white people readily fit in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See institutional racism for related concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tagalog
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced tah-GAH-log. The official language of the Philippines and one of many local/regional dialects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taipeng Revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the bloodiest conflicts in world history; a long civil war in China contemporaneous with the American Civil War, possibly killing ~20 million.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Led by a Chinese national who believed he was Jesus' younger brother; cited as a continuing theme illustrating the central government's fear of separatist movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tao
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'Dow.' The ever-changing energy of the universe that flows in nature; in Taoism, Tao is unknowable and cannot be defined; in Confucianism, Tao is correct conduct stemming from universal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taoism, Daoism
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'DOW-ism.' A school of philosophical and religious teachings stemming from Tao; one of the major religions in China.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppressed during Maoist rule and later flourished; use either spelling as appropriate to context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tejano
rubrics_metrics.description: A Texan of Mexican descent; derives from 'Coahuiltejano.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tejano culture includes folk music synthesized from European and Mexican styles and contributes to Tex-Mex cuisine. Historical bilingualism shaped the Tejano language.

rubrics_metrics.name: telenovela
rubrics_metrics.description: A limited-run television drama popular in Latin America with episodes five to six days a week; average ~120 episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to U.S. soap operas but distinctive due to fixed run time and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thai names
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically personal name first, family name second, with long multi-syllable names, especially if Chinese.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On second reference, the personal name is sometimes used.

rubrics_metrics.name: third gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Term often used in anthropological studies to refer to identities other than man or woman that appear across cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See androgyne, agender, genderqueer, non-binary gender for related terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third World
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally distinguished nations aligned with neither West nor East during the Cold War; commonly used to describe underdeveloped countries of Africa, Asia and Latin America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using due to negative connotations; prefer 'developing countries.' Use only in quotes if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiananmen Square
rubrics_metrics.description: Vast public square in Beijing; in 1989 up to a million protesters demonstrated for democracy, prompting a lethal crackdown on June 4 with deaths at least in the hundreds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The crackdown is a central event in modern Chinese history; number of deaths still unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: tolerance (drug)
rubrics_metrics.description: Condition where higher drug doses are required to produce the same effect achieved during initial use, often leading to dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torah
rubrics_metrics.description: Jewish sacred writings in the first five books of the Hebrew Bible; copied by specialized scribes onto parchment scrolls and treated with care and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also used to describe larger body of Jewish law and Scripture.

rubrics_metrics.name: totem
rubrics_metrics.description: A representation of a person or likeness (animal/plant) revered by a tribe or group; part of many American Indian and African religious practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tourette syndrome/Tourette's syndrome/Tourette's disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: A neurological disorder characterized by tics — sudden, purposeless, rapid movements or vocalizations that are recurrent, involuntary and non-rhythmic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Tourette syndrome' (no possessive, no capitalization of syndrome). Refer to someone as having Tourette syndrome only if relevant and formally diagnosed by a licensed medical professional. Use people-first language: 'a person with Tourette syndrome' or 'a person diagnosed with Tourette syndrome.' Avoid the acronym TS. For more info, see Tourette Syndrome Association, NAMI fact sheet, or NINDS fact sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: towelhead
rubrics_metrics.description: A slur used to describe South Asians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using this term.

rubrics_metrics.name: tranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Often a pejorative term for a transgender person, though reclaimed by some.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offensive when used as an epithet and should be avoided except in quotes or when someone self-identifies with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental Meditation
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of meditation popularized by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi beginning in 1955.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviated TM is acceptable on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: transfeminine
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes people assigned male at birth who identify with a feminine gender identity more than masculine; not interchangeable with trans woman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can describe gender expression or identity. Masculine equivalent is transmasculine.

rubrics_metrics.name: transgender
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals whose gender identity and/or expression may not match physical/sexual characteristics or sex assigned at birth; includes some cross-dressers, drag performers and intersex individuals who identify as transgender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the name and personal pronouns consistent with how the person lives publicly; ask which term the source prefers when possible. Do not use 'transgendered.' Avoid using transgender as a noun; use 'transgender people,' 'transgender man,' or 'transgender woman.' In space-limited contexts (e.g., headlines), 'trans' as a shorthand adjectival form is acceptable. See entries on gender transition, intersex, sexual reassignment and external resources (NLGJA toolbox, GLAAD Media Reference Guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: transmasculine
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes people assigned female at birth who identify with a masculine gender identity more than feminine; not interchangeable with trans man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can describe gender expression or identity; includes non-binary, gender fluid, genderqueer people assigned female at birth whose gender falls in a more masculine range. Feminine equivalent is transfeminine.

rubrics_metrics.name: transracial
rubrics_metrics.description: Across or crossing racial boundaries; often used in adoption to describe families where a child is adopted by parents of a different race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 2015 the term applied to Rachel Dolezal controversy (a white woman identifying as black). Context matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: transsexual
rubrics_metrics.description: An outdated term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid in favor of 'transgender' and 'transgender people' unless a person or community prefers the term; term can carry misleading medical connotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: transvestite
rubrics_metrics.description: An outdated term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using this term.

rubrics_metrics.name: treatment/treatment center/rehab center/detox center
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment (per American Society of Addiction Medicine) is any planned, intentional intervention to achieve and maintain sobriety, physical and mental health and maximum functional ability for alcoholism/drug dependency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A treatment center is usually run by psychiatric or medical professionals. Use 'treatment' for medical interventions and 'treatment center' instead of 'rehab' or 'detox center.' A person enrolled in a treatment center should be referred to as a 'patient.'

rubrics_metrics.name: tribal affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should identify Indigenous people by their specific tribes, nations or communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines and text should refer to tribes by their proper names rather than catch-all phrases like 'Oklahoma Native American Tribe' or 'Native American group.' Tribal nations are diverse; failing to use the actual tribal name is inaccurate, unfair, and erases identity. Examples of incorrect vs correct headline usage are provided. (Updated January 2024.)

rubrics_metrics.name: tribal council
rubrics_metrics.description: The governing body of a tribe, usually elected by adult members; headed by an elected chairperson, president, chief or governor recognized as the leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The council performs legislative aspects of tribal government. See American Indian, Native American, tribe.

rubrics_metrics.name: tribal warfare
rubrics_metrics.description: A Eurocentric term for ethnic conflict among people of color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'tribal warfare.' Use 'ethnic conflicts' or 'civil wars' as appropriate. Example: Rwanda (Hutus/Tutsis) was called tribal warfare incorrectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: tribe
rubrics_metrics.description: Use with caution; prefer 'nation' or 'ethnic group' except for specific entities that call themselves a 'tribe' or in contexts like tribal council on a reservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the U.S., many Native Americans prefer 'nation' because of treaties and government-to-government relationships. Some prefer national affiliation (e.g., Navajo, Hopi, Cherokee). In Africa, avoid referring to ethnic groups as tribes. See American Indian, Native American, Native.

rubrics_metrics.name: trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological triggers are words, images or sounds that activate phobias, panic attacks or flashbacks to trauma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News covering sensitive topics (abuse, assault, addiction, suicide, combat, violence) can contain scenarios that deeply affect audiences. Trigger warnings communicate that content may produce unpredictable reactions and give audiences a choice. Some object to trigger warnings as patronizing. Educators should consider alerting students if content contains graphic descriptions; warnings may be appropriate in broadcast/digital material. Don't use 'trigger warning' in a flip or casual way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Key doctrine in Christianity: God, the Son and the Holy Spirit together make the one Godhead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exact nature/definition of the Trinity was central to the split between Eastern and Western Christian churches.

rubrics_metrics.name: trust land
rubrics_metrics.description: Land held by the United States for the use and benefit of American Indian tribes; virtually all trust land is on reservations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribes can also purchase land and petition the federal government to hold it in trust to protect from encroachment or seizure. See reservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: turban
rubrics_metrics.description: A head covering in desert or hot climates that does not necessarily have ethnic or religious significance and is not solely Arab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People wear turbans for different reasons; many types exist. Sikh men wear turbans that peak at the forehead to care for uncut hair, promote equality, and declare identity. Turbans are distinctive in India where Sikhs are a minority; some Sikhs have been attacked when assumed to be Muslim. Most Muslims do not wear turbans, though some religious figures may. Shape varies by country. See Sikhism.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. territories
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States has five major permanently inhabited territories: American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People born in all territories but American Samoa are U.S. citizens; people born in American Samoa are U.S. nationals but not citizens and must apply for citizenship if desired. The entry lists the demonyms for each territory (American Samoans, Guamians, Northern Mariana Islanders, Puerto Ricans, Virgin Islanders).

rubrics_metrics.name: ultra-Orthodox
rubrics_metrics.description: Term sometimes applied to strictly observant Jews such as Hasidim, distinguished by style of dress, appearance and attention to ritual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some communities (e.g., Lubavitch Hasidim) find the term offensive; Agudath Israel objects. Other groups do not. 'Haredi/Charedi' is an alternative but not widely known. 'Modern Orthodox' is a separate, acceptable category.

rubrics_metrics.name: uncle
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cultures, 'uncle' is a term of respect, not necessarily a family relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an Arab American might call an older Arab male 'uncle' ('ammo'). Recognize cultural uses beyond blood relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncle Tom
rubrics_metrics.description: A term of contempt based on the character in Uncle Tom's Cabin, meaning a black person who treats whites as superiors or is eager to please them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply the term to a person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncle Tom’s Cabin (or Life Among the Lowly)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 1852 antislavery novel by Harriet Beecher Stowe that increased sentiment against slavery; main character Uncle Tom was pious and faithful; novel credited by some historians with helping prompt the Civil War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides historical context for the term 'Uncle Tom.' See slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: unconscious bias
rubrics_metrics.description: See implicit bias, unconscious bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underground Railroad
rubrics_metrics.description: A vast network pre-Civil War that helped free slaves in the U.S.; peaked in the early 1830s and involved safe houses and transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated 100,000 slaves freed; notable figures include John Fairfield, Levi Coffin, and Harriet Tubman (made 19 trips and escorted over 300 slaves). Slaves used songs to relay messages of escape.

rubrics_metrics.name: undocumented immigrant, undocumented individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred terms to 'illegal alien,' 'illegal immigrant' or 'illegal(s)'; describe immigration status of people without federal documentation to show legal right to work/visit/live in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term avoids dehumanizing connotations. Note: Feb. 2021 USCIS memo instructed leadership to stop using 'illegal alien/alien/undocumented alien' and instead use 'noncitizen,' 'undocumented noncitizen,' or 'undocumented individual.' Updated Feb. 17, 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: undocumented worker
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred term to 'illegal alien,' 'illegal immigrant' or 'illegal(s)' when describing immigration status related to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification Church
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal name: Holy Spirit Association for the Unification of World Christianity, founded by Rev. Sun Myung Moon in 1954 in South Korea; 'Unification Church' acceptable in references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moon launched it after being excommunicated by Presbyterian Church of Korea. Members are often called 'Moonies' (derogatory); preferred term is 'Unificationists.' Use 'Moonies' only in direct quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitarian Universalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Association encourages a wide spectrum of belief, including theists and atheists; members do not believe Jesus was divine and are not considered Christians though they may welcome Christians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They employ a congregational form of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Church of Christ
rubrics_metrics.description: A mainline Protestant denomination and the largest of Congregationalist denominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'church' applies only to individual local churches. Clergy are 'ministers'; 'Pastor' is used if a minister leads a congregation. On first reference, use 'the Rev.' before the name; on second reference, use only the last name.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Methodist Church
rubrics_metrics.description: The largest Methodist denomination and the second-largest Protestant body in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officially 'The United Methodist Church' but Religion Stylebook follows Associated Press practice in not capitalizing 'The' as part of the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Negro College Fund
rubrics_metrics.description: Nation’s largest, oldest and most comprehensive minority higher education assistance organization; provides funds, scholarships and internships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May use 'UNCF' on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity Church
rubrics_metrics.description: A denomination that promotes 'practical Christianity' and is primary in the 'New Thought' movement, which teaches monism and belief in universal creative energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some adherents accept traditional Christian beliefs about Jesus; many do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Untouchables
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical term for castes once called 'untouchables.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Dalit' (capitalized) as more respectful and current term. Note M.K. Gandhi coined 'Harijan' but contemporary preferred usage is Dalit.

rubrics_metrics.name: urban
rubrics_metrics.description: Widely used euphemism for Black people or neighborhoods; may connote stereotypes of poverty and crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'urban' with caution; acceptable in neutral contexts (e.g., 'housing values in the urban neighborhood are rising'). Be aware of exclusion of people with mobility disabilities when using terms like 'walking distance' (see walkability entry). Note that in 2020 some organizations ceased using 'urban' for music genres and labels due to evolving connotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: urban music, urban contemporary
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Urban' and 'urban contemporary' used as catchall terms categorizing rhythmic music by Black artists, segregating artists from mass-market platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In June 2020, some labels and the Recording Academy removed or renamed 'urban' categories/labels (examples provided). Consider more specific genre labels rather than 'urban.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Urdu
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the official languages of Pakistan; also spoken in parts of India (e.g., Uttar Pradesh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urdu is used in ghazals and written in a Perso-Arabic alphabet adapted from Arabic script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vatican, Vatican City
rubrics_metrics.description: A 108-acre city-state that is the temporal headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church where the pope and administrative clergy live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vatican City is an independent state in the center of Rome with its own flag, coins, postage stamps, media, train station and police (Swiss Guard). Popes were once temporal rulers; after Italy's unification in 1870 and later in 1929 the Vatican regained recognized status via concordat. Vatican City stands alone in datelines. For more, see official Vatican website.

rubrics_metrics.name: vegetative state/comatose/non-response
rubrics_metrics.description: A vegetative state is absence of responsiveness/consciousness with no awareness of environment; minimally conscious state shows some awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid calling a person a 'vegetable.' Prefer precise medical terminology or terms like 'comatose' or 'non-responsive.' If using 'vegetative state,' use people-first language (e.g., 'a person in a vegetative state'). Avoid dehumanizing terms like 'veg' or 'vegetable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: veiling
rubrics_metrics.description: A religious practice related to Islam, not specifically Arab; varies by region and class and is not universally observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some see veiling as denigrating women; many women say it liberates them. Governments have at times banned or required veiling. Within families, practices may vary. Hijab is the practice of modesty; recognize diversity of motivations and meaning. Most Arab Americans dress like other Americans; don't assume veiling equals oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: victim, suffering from, afflicted with, stricken with
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid making assumptions about how someone with mental illness or other conditions is handling life; use value-neutral terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not preferred: 'She suffers from anxiety.' Preferred: 'She's being treated for an anxiety disorder' or 'She is diagnosed with an anxiety disorder.' Use people-first, factual phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: victim, survivor
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate exists around use of 'victim' vs 'survivor' in sexual assault and domestic violence contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, ask sources which terms they prefer. 'Victim' conveys someone was injured by a crime but can imply passivity and narrow identity; 'survivor' can convey agency and resilience but is also one-dimensional. Alternative wording examples: 'a person who was subjected to sexual violence,' 'a person who was sexually assaulted,' 'a person who survived sexual abuse,' and 'complainant' for court contexts. These alternatives depict the event without defining the person's whole life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vietnamese names
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically family name first, personal name last; on second reference, the personal name is sometimes used. In the U.S., Western word order is common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vodou, Voodoo
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious tradition born in West Africa derived from animism, ancestor worship and polytheism; merged with Roman Catholic beliefs in the Caribbean and Gulf Coast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Vodou' (capitalized) in academic and Haitian community contexts. Other spellings (Vodun, Voodoo, voodoo) exist; generic uses (e.g., 'voodoo economics') can be offensive — avoid except in direct quotes. Note AP Style still uses 'Voodoo.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting Rights Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Enacted Aug. 6, 1965; empowered federal government to oversee voter registration and elections in jurisdictions that used discriminatory tests or had low registration/turnout; banned discriminatory literacy tests and expanded voting rights for non-English speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects were wide; by 1968 nearly 60% of eligible Blacks in Mississippi were registered. The Act was extended in 1970, 1975, and 1982 and had a major impact on electing Black lawmakers, despite setbacks and debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: walking distance, walkability, walkable
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms used in real estate and urban planning to describe pedestrian access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware these may exclude people who use wheelchairs or have mobility disabilities. Prefer 'accessible' or 'pedestrian friendly' to include people who use wheelchairs (they are pedestrians).

rubrics_metrics.name: West Indies
rubrics_metrics.description: Group of islands in the Caribbean Sea including Bahamas, Cuba, Jamaica, Haiti, Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, U.S. Virgin Islands, Leeward and Windward Islands, Guyana, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named because Spanish explorers mistakenly thought they had sailed to India.

rubrics_metrics.name: wheelchair/wheelchair-bound/confined to a wheelchair
rubrics_metrics.description: People who use mobility equipment such as wheelchairs, scooters or canes consider equipment part of personal space and have widely different disabilities/abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe a person as 'someone who uses a wheelchair,' followed by an explanation if necessary. Avoid 'confined to a wheelchair' or 'wheelchair-bound' as these are misleading, dehumanizing, and inaccurate — wheelchairs can liberate people and users are not permanently confined to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: White flight
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden or gradual large-scale migration of White people from areas becoming more racially or ethnoculturally diverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: White privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages for people with white skin, including those they might not know about; can be a product of systemic racism and manifest economically, socially or educationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: freedom from barriers, suspicions, or expectations that non-White people face; differential assumptions about success. See institutional racism, systemic racism for related concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: White, U.S. Census definition of
rubrics_metrics.description: Census Bureau (per 1997 OMB standards) defines White as 'a person having origins in any of the original peoples of Europe, the Middle East, or North Africa.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The racial categories reflect a social definition of race recognized in the U.S., not attempts to define race biologically, anthropologically, or genetically. Categories include racial and national origin/sociocultural groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: White, white
rubrics_metrics.description: People who share lineage traceable to Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't use 'Caucasian.' Discussion exists about capitalizing 'White' and 'Black' — many style guides changed to capitalize 'Black' in 2020 but most still lowercase 'white.' Organizations differ; AP initially chose not to capitalize 'White' while others recommend capitalization for parity. Monitor evolving usage and newsroom policy.
